title: Pairwise and Mutual Independence
quickIdea: For three events, pairwise independence is three products. Mutual independence needs a fourth, P(A and B and C) = P(A)P(B)P(C), and pairwise independence does not give it.
remember: n events are mutually independent when every sub-family of size 2 or more satisfies the product rule: 2^n - n - 1 separate equations.
Mutual independence implies pairwise independence; the converse fails, and the standard counterexample is small enough to memorise.
The counterexample: two fair coins; A = head on the first, B = head on the second, C = the two coins differ. Each pair is independent and P(A and B and C) = 0, not 1/8.
Pairwise independence is not enough to multiply three probabilities, and not enough to add variances of three terms.
In a GATE MSQ, an option that says 'pairwise independent' is weaker than 'independent', and the difference is exactly the triple product.
When a question says only 'A and B', the two-event definition is all that is needed; do not import the three-event machinery into a two-event question.

example.prompt: Two fair coins are tossed. A = head on the first, B = head on the second, C = the coins show different faces. Test all three pairs, then the triple.
example.work: The space is HH, HT, TH, TT; A = {HH, HT}, B = {HH, TH}, C = {HT, TH}, each of probability 1/2. P(A and B) = P(HH) = 1/4 = (1/2)(1/2); P(A and C) = P(HT) = 1/4; P(B and C) = P(TH) = 1/4. So every pair passes. But A and B and C would need HH, HT and TH at once, which is impossible: P(A and B and C) = 0, against the required (1/2)^3 = 1/8.
example.answer: Pairwise independent but not mutually independent.

gateAngle: No CSE previous-year question in this topic asks for mutual independence of three events, so this card is P2 and rests on the standard construction and on recomputation rather than on a verified question.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: In the coin construction above, which single number shows that mutual independence fails?
variations.answer: P(A and B and C) = 0, which should be 1/8.
variations.why: All three pairwise products hold, so the only remaining condition is the triple product, and it fails as badly as possible.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Three events have P(A) = P(B) = P(C) = 1/2, all three pairwise intersections of probability 1/4, and P(A and B and C) = 1/8. Are they mutually independent?
variations.why: All four required products hold: three pairwise and one triple. This is the case the counterexample fails to reach.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: How many product conditions must n events satisfy to be mutually independent?
variations.why: One condition for each sub-family of size 2 or more; there are 2^n sub-families, of which n are singletons and one is empty.

trap.what: Checking only the pairwise products and concluding mutual independence.
trap.why: Pairwise independence constrains every two-way overlap but says nothing about the three-way overlap, which can be forced to zero by the design of the events.
trap.counterexample: The two-coin construction: three pairwise products of 1/4 all hold, yet the triple intersection is empty.

check.question: In the two-coin construction, what is P(A and B and C)?
check.explanation: C requires the coins to differ while A and B require both to be heads; no outcome satisfies all three, so the triple probability is 0 against the required 1/8.
